global.headline: MEDIATORS FLOAT 10-DAY IRAN CEASEFIRE AS US STRIKES ENTER TENTH NIGHT AND HOUTHIS FORCE SAUDI TANKERS TO TURN BACK
summary: Regional mediators — reportedly including Qatar, Egypt and Pakistan — have presented Washington and Tehran with a proposal for a 10-day ceasefire aimed at reviving last month's Islamabad MOU, Axios and Reuters reported. The plan would fully reopen both Hormuz shipping lanes — the southern route through Omani waters and the northern route through Iranian waters — free of Iranian attacks and the US naval blockade respectively, giving both sides a 10-day window to negotiate a longer-term arrangement governing the strait. The Trump administration is said to be exploring the proposal and has urged Israel not to take steps that would close the diplomatic window, though Washington is reportedly pushing for a longer ceasefire than 10 days. It is the first concrete de-escalation proposal since the ceasefire's practical collapse in early July.

On the ground, the war showed no sign of pausing: CENTCOM struck Iran for a tenth consecutive night, hitting command centres, maritime-attack capabilities, missile/drone launch sites and air-defence systems from the Hormuz littoral to Shiraz and Isfahan, saying the wave was designed to "further degrade Iranian military capabilities used to attack commercial shipping." A merchant tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile early Tuesday roughly 8 nautical miles off Oman's Kumzar, forcing its crew to abandon ship; Greek operator Dynacom Tankers said two of its managed vessels were separately hit by projectiles off Oman. Kuwait said Iranian strikes again hit several of its power-generation and desalination plants, sparking fires that were later extinguished — the second time in under a week Kuwait's water/power infrastructure has been targeted. Testifying before the Senate Appropriations Committee amid protester interruptions, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth put the war's cost at US$37.5 billion so far, up from earlier estimates, as the administration seeks funding on top of a $95 billion GOP war-budget package; the confirmed US military death toll stands at 17, with nearly 100 more injured this month (96% have returned to duty).

Yemen's Houthis turned their newly declared maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia into concrete disruption Tuesday: two tankers that had just loaded Saudi crude for China and India at the Red Sea port of Yanbu reversed course toward the Suez Canal rather than risk the Bab el-Mandeb strait. Israel, still on the sidelines, is drawing up contingency plans of its own — Netanyahu convened a limited security-cabinet meeting Monday night to review scenarios in which Israel could be pulled in (a US request, an Iranian trigger, or a pre-emptive strike) — but for now says it has "no interest in joining the campaign," per Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.
global.geopolitical: A live ceasefire proposal running in parallel with a tenth night of strikes, a second Houthi-driven chokepoint disruption and Israel quietly gaming out its own entry all at once shows a war that is simultaneously escalating and searching for an exit — whether the 10-day window becomes a genuine off-ramp or another missed one may hinge on whether Washington accepts a shorter ceasefire than it wants.
global.socioeconomic: Brent held near $89/barrel and WTI above $82 as the Houthi-driven Red Sea disruption compounds an already near-frozen Hormuz, while Hegseth's $37.5bn cost estimate and the fresh Kuwait infrastructure damage put a hard number on a war whose energy-price and shipping-insurance spillover keeps feeding into the same cost-of-living pressures visible in Singapore's record COE premiums and electricity tariffs.

global.headline: ZELENSKY SACKS ARMY CHIEF SYRSKY, NAMES FEDOROV ALLY DRAPATY, AMID DAYS OF PROTEST
summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky dismissed commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrsky, 60 — who had led Ukraine's armed forces since 2024 and directed the defence of Kyiv at the start of the 2022 invasion — after days of street protests demanding accountability for the sacking of defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who accused Syrsky of forcing him out and blocking his attempted military reforms. Zelensky named Major General Mykhailo Drapaty, an ally of Fedorov, as the new commander-in-chief, and said he had separately offered Fedorov a "decent post" overseeing the state's technological programmes.

The reshuffle resolves the immediate leadership crisis but leaves open whether the protest movement — which revealed an unprecedented public split in the military over wartime strategy — is satisfied, and whether Drapaty can hold together the reform agenda Fedorov was pursuing.
global.geopolitical: Removing his own top general under sustained street pressure, rather than the reverse, is a striking reversal of the civil-military balance Zelensky has otherwise carefully managed since 2022, and a signal to Kyiv's allies that internal cohesion — not just the front line — is now a live variable in the war.
global.socioeconomic: A leadership change atop Ukraine's armed forces, following directly from a fight over military-reform pace, adds uncertainty to the drone-warfare and mobilisation programmes Fedorov had championed, at a moment allied military aid and domestic recruitment are already under strain.

global.headline: GUYANA FERRY DEATH TOLL RISES TO 41 AS CAPTAIN HELD OVER CAPSIZED VESSEL CARRYING 179
summary: The death toll from the capsized ferry MV Barima off Guyana's coast rose to 41 on Tuesday as 14 more bodies were recovered, with 77 people rescued so far; the vessel — built in 1939 — was carrying 179 people from Georgetown to the north-western village of Port Kaituma when it capsized over the weekend. Authorities say an inaccurate passenger manifest and alleged drug use by crew members may have contributed to the disaster; the captain and other crew are in police custody.
global.geopolitical: A near-century-old vessel, an unreliable passenger count and alleged crew impairment together point to a systemic maritime-safety failure in Guyana's remote coastal transport network rather than a one-off accident, raising pressure on the government to tighten licensing and manifest enforcement.
global.socioeconomic: Port Kaituma's isolated communities depend on ferries like the Barima for basic transport and goods; a prolonged suspension of the route while the investigation proceeds would compound hardship in an already underserved region.

global.headline: INDIA'S "COCKROACH" PROTESTERS VOW TO CONTINUE AS CRACKDOWN INJURES NEARLY 180, COURT ORDERS WANGCHUK MOVED
summary: India's youth-led Cockroach movement said it would keep protesting a day after a police crackdown that Delhi Police said injured nearly 180 people, including 118 security personnel and 60 protesters; video of officers beating and dragging away demonstrators, some seen crying and pleading, spread widely on social media. About 200 protesters gathered Tuesday morning at Jantar Mantar in a monsoon drizzle, continuing to demand the education minister's resignation over a string of exam-system scandals.

The Delhi High Court ruled Tuesday that hunger-striking activist Sonam Wangchuk, 59 — forcibly hospitalised by police over the weekend after three weeks without food — could be moved from a government hospital to a private facility, after his wife petitioned the court alleging he was being held in "illegal detention."
global.geopolitical: A court intervening to override a forced-hospitalisation order, on top of a triple-digit injury count from the crackdown itself, signals institutional friction between India's judiciary and its policing response — a check that could either de-escalate the standoff or harden protesters' sense that the courts, not the government, are their only recourse.
global.socioeconomic: Recurring exam-system failures feeding a movement large enough to sustain 180 injuries and keep regathering the next morning reflect real structural stakes for India's youth competing for scarce public-sector and university places, a pressure point no single minister's resignation would resolve.

global.headline: TRUMP SAYS NETANYAHU "WILL NOT BE ARRESTED" IN US AFTER MAMDANI FLOATS ICC WARRANT ENFORCEMENT
summary: President Trump said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu "will not be arrested, in any way, shape, or form, while in the United States," rebuffing New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who said his administration was in "active conversation" about whether city authorities could detain Netanyahu when he visits New York in September for the UN General Assembly. Netanyahu has been subject to an International Criminal Court arrest warrant for alleged war crimes; neither the US nor Israel are ICC members, and the US has no obligation to enforce the court's warrants.
global.geopolitical: A sitting US president publicly guaranteeing a foreign leader's immunity from a city-level enforcement threat underscores Washington's continued rejection of ICC jurisdiction over Israeli officials, while handing Mamdani a high-profile platform to press the question regardless of the outcome.
global.socioeconomic: The dispute is largely symbolic with no direct economic channel, but it keeps US-Israel solidarity a live domestic political fault line inside the country whose military posture is simultaneously shaping Gulf oil-supply risk.

singapore.headline: MAN, 66, CHARGED WITH MURDER AFTER FATAL LENGKOK BAHRU NEIGHBOUR FIGHT
summary: Koh Ah Hwee, 66, was charged with murder Tuesday after a 59-year-old neighbour died following a fight at Block 55 Lengkok Bahru on Monday afternoon. Police were alerted at about 4:45pm and found the victim lying motionless at the 16th-floor lift lobby; he was taken to hospital and later died. Preliminary investigations indicate the victim retrieved a stick from his flat while his neighbour armed himself with a knife before the fight, in which the victim was stabbed in the abdomen; residents say the two men, who lived several units apart, had a longstanding feud and would argue regularly.
singapore.geopolitical: A neighbour dispute escalating to a fatal stabbing despite years of apparent friction beforehand raises familiar questions about how much earlier intervention — mediation, town-council involvement, police welfare checks — could have de-escalated a conflict that was evidently visible to the wider block.
singapore.socioeconomic: Long-running unresolved disputes in dense public housing carry a real safety cost when informal community mechanisms fail, a recurring theme in Singapore's HDB estates that this case is likely to sharpen rather than resolve on its own.

singapore.headline: SAF CAPTAIN, 26, CHARGED WITH POSSESSING CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE MATERIAL
summary: Dylan Yoon Ker Tern, a 26-year-old Singapore Armed Forces captain, was charged in court on 15 July with possessing at least eight items of sexually explicit child abuse material and 20 obscene films, allegedly at a Geylang East flat on 21 August 2025. MINDEF confirmed to The Straits Times on Monday that Yoon has been suspended from all duties pending the outcome of the case.
singapore.geopolitical: A serving officer facing child-abuse-material charges tests the SAF's internal vetting and disciplinary processes at a time institutional integrity across statutory boards and uniformed services is already under scrutiny from other recent cases.
singapore.socioeconomic: Suspension pending trial reflects a now-standard institutional response to such charges, but each case adds to a steady drumbeat of online child-exploitation prosecutions in Singapore that welfare and law-enforcement agencies continue to flag as a persistent, not isolated, problem.

singapore.headline: PDPC MAKES AI-SPECIFIC DATA NOTIFICATIONS MANDATORY FOR FIRMS TRAINING AI MODELS
summary: From 20 July, organisations using personal data to train generative AI models must give consumers AI-specific notifications rather than relying on broad privacy-statement language such as "new product development," under advisory guidelines the Personal Data Protection Commission issued following a month-long public consultation (2 June–1 July). Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo announced the move at the Singapore Data Festival, with PDPC citing risks that sensitive data — children's records, health and credit information — could be exposed or reconstructed from AI models once absorbed into training, and the difficulty of later removing or correcting it.
singapore.geopolitical: Formalising AI-specific consent norms ahead of most regional peers gives Singapore an early template other jurisdictions may look to as generative-AI regulation catches up with deployment, reinforcing its positioning as a trusted, rules-based digital hub.
singapore.socioeconomic: Firms training AI models on Singapore user data now face fresh compliance overhead precisely as they scale AI investment, a cost businesses will weigh against the transparency benefits to consumers whose sensitive data is hardest to scrub once ingested into a model.

singapore.headline: REMAINING 127 CHARGES AGAINST HIN LEONG FOUNDER O.K. LIM WITHDRAWN
summary: A district court granted O.K. Lim (Lim Oon Kuin), 84, a discharge amounting to an acquittal on 17 July for the remaining 127 charges he faced, including cheating counts, after prosecutors withdrew them and issued a stern warning instead, The Straits Times reported Monday. The discharge means Lim cannot be prosecuted again for the same offences. He is currently serving a 13.5-year sentence — reduced from an original 17.5 years on appeal in March — for his earlier conviction over the collapse of oil trader Hin Leong.
singapore.geopolitical: Closing out the remaining charges against Lim, even as two smaller civil claims from Hin Leong's liquidators against Deloitte remain live, draws a line under one of Singapore's most-watched corporate-fraud sagas and signals prosecutors judged further pursuit not to be in the public interest given his existing sentence and age.
singapore.socioeconomic: The withdrawal closes the criminal side of a collapse that cost creditors billions and reshaped scrutiny of Singapore's commodity-trading sector, leaving the smaller live Deloitte claims as the last avenue for creditors seeking further recovery.

word.definition: To dismiss summarily from a position of command or authority, especially in disgrace; historically, to strip a military officer of rank.
word.example: Zelensky cashiered his own commander-in-chief, Oleksandr Syrsky, amid days of protest over a defence minister's ouster, even as mediators dangled a fragile 10-day Iran ceasefire against the backdrop of a tenth straight night of US strikes.
